appraisal_events.evidence: J’étais torturé par l’incessante reprise du désir toujours plus anxieux... ; il feigns indifference on the telephone (« Est-ce que vous venez ? demandai-je d’un ton indifférent »), invents a rheumatism to hide his misery, and concludes that Albertine’s life is « organisée comme des fortifications de campagne » et « camouflées », so that « je n’apprendrais jamais rien ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The passage is dominated by the narrator's anxious, dependent waiting and by his recognition that Albertine is unreachable and lying, which the narration explicitly endorses as torment and as an anticipation of « longues souffrances »; Albertine correspondingly holds the emotional leverage, conceding her visit only on her own terms.

appraisal_events.evidence: « vous en êtes au même point que le jour où vous êtes arrivée à Paris, aussi bien pour vous connaître en choses de toilette que pour bien prononcer les mots et ne pas faire de cuirs », followed at once by « Et ce reproche était particulièrement stupide ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator strikes back at Françoise's mockery of Albertine with a cruel, class-inflected put-down, but the narration immediately disqualifies the reproach as stupid, so the snub rebounds on its author rather than lowering Françoise.

status_effects.explanation: He is locally reduced to anxious dependence: he rewires the telephone, sits immobile listening, dissimulates his suffering, and ends convinced he can never know where Albertine is.
His retaliatory cruelty toward Françoise is explicitly labelled stupid by the narration, which lowers him rather than her.
She holds the leverage throughout: she is elsewhere and enjoying it, lies about the note, offers and withdraws her visit, and comes only when it suits her, while he must conceal his need.

She is credited with an art rivalling la Berma's, her report « Mieux vaut tard que jamais ! » pierces the narrator's heart, and his counterstroke is disowned as stupid, leaving her the effective winner of the exchange.

ambiguities: Albertine's telephone call and arrival produce an explicit « joie profonde », but the text at once qualifies it (« Elle ne demeura pas longtemps sans mélange ») and the surrounding body is governed by anxiety, lying, and jealousy; the passage is read here as dominantly negative rather than as a renewal, since no intimacy or mutual receptivity is realized.

Françoise is simultaneously admired (« avec admiration et fureur », the Berma comparison), mocked as a persecution-obsessed reporter, and insulted; the narrator's admiration is half-ironic, so her local gain rests mainly on the narrator's self-condemnation rather than on unqualified endorsement.
